title: How to Choose an LLM Observability Platform for AI Agents
summary: Choose an LLM observability platform for AI agents by testing the same traces, checking data portability, and comparing debugging, evals, and costs.
body_markdown:
To choose an LLM observability platform, compare how each tool records your agent runs and helps you diagnose their outcomes. A procurement agent gives you several different tests: create_po


fails because an account is on credit hold, another run orders the wrong quantity without raising an error, and finance needs cost per customer. A tracing checkbox doesn't tell you whether those questions are answerable.


This guide builds on[agent observability](https://laminar.sh/article/agent-observability) with a selection protocol: send copies of the same runs to each candidate, check their interpretation, and ask every tool the same questions. Laminar receives a copy in the worked example. The method remains useful if you keep your current platform.


## How to choose an LLM observability platform#


Start with three to five questions your team actually asks. Use the wording from an incident report or Slack thread, then identify the evidence and operation each answer requires. For the procurement agent, the list was: why did run f5cdfeb4


fail and at which step, which runs called search_catalog


more than five times, what each customer cost last week, which "successful" runs ordered the wrong quantity, and whether those runs can become regression cases.


Team question Evidence needed Required operation


Why did this run fail? Tool arguments, results, errors Inspect the failing step


Which runs repeated a search? Named tool spans Count calls across runs


What did each customer cost? Customer ID, model, tokens Group and sum costs


Which successful runs were wrong? Requested and actual outcomes Evaluate semantic correctness


Can we prevent this regression? Inputs and expected behavior Create a regression case


Decide which answers are mandatory before opening a vendor demo. Record how each candidate answers them, including manual exports and workarounds. A tool that needs a notebook for every investigation may still fit, but that work belongs in the decision.


### When a shorter evaluation is enough#


Hard constraints can narrow the shortlist first. If traces must remain on your infrastructure, check deployment options before testing the UI. An existing Datadog deployment makes its LLM Observability product a reasonable first candidate. For a LangGraph-only stack, examine the LangChain-native workflow early.


Use the[agent observability platform roundup](https://laminar.sh/article/top-6-agent-observability-platforms) for that shortlist. Short, single-call features may need only a capture check rather than a production trial.


Without production traffic, run a synthetic proof of concept with injected failures, such as malformed tool output or a retry loop. A vendor-assisted POC can work well if you control the workflow, failures and acceptance criteria.


## Check portability beyond OpenTelemetry support#


OpenTelemetry can reduce the instrumentation work needed to switch backends. It does not make every part of an observability platform portable.


OTLP standardizes transport. Attribute interpretation still varies: the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions remain marked Development, and backends accept different combinations of GenAI, OpenInference, OpenLLMetry and vendor-specific keys. These documented inputs were checked on November 25, 2026:


Platform Core license Documented OTLP Attribute inputs


Laminar Apache-2.0 gRPC, HTTP/protobuf, HTTP/JSON GenAI, older OpenLLMetry, lmnr.*


Langfuse MIT; ee/


excluded HTTP/protobuf, HTTP/JSON GenAI, OpenInference, langfuse.*


Phoenix Elastic License 2.0 gRPC, HTTP/protobuf OpenInference, converted GenAI


MLflow Apache-2.0 HTTP GenAI, OpenInference, other translators


LangSmith Proprietary HTTP GenAI, OpenInference, OpenLLMetry, langsmith.*


Braintrust Proprietary HTTP GenAI, OpenInference, braintrust.*


Phoenix is source-available under Elastic License 2.0, not an Apache- or MIT-licensed option. Proprietary licensing does not rule out private deployment: LangSmith offers self-hosting as an Enterprise add-on, while Braintrust offers BYOC on Enterprise.


Check feature entitlements separately from repository licenses. For example, Laminar's[Signals](https://laminar.sh/docs/signals/introduction) require paid Cloud access or an enterprise license when self-hosted; they are absent from the OSS build.


For portability, test whether messages, tool calls and business identifiers survive export in usable fields. Also check migration paths for datasets, saved queries and evaluation definitions. An exporter change alone does not migrate those workflows. The[OpenTelemetry for AI agents guide](https://laminar.sh/article/opentelemetry-for-ai-agents) covers instrumentation and attributes in more detail.


## Send matching runs to each candidate#


Choose the route that fits your existing instrumentation. Approve both destinations before copying prompts, tool results or customer data. Set a trial budget and end date: another export adds traffic and can add ingestion charges.


The routing tests below used local backends. Hosted endpoint values come from Laminar's documentation, not a hosted-endpoint test.


### Option 1: fan out through a Collector#


If your application already exports OTLP, configure one Collector exporter per candidate. Each receives a copy of the incoming spans. This example targets Laminar Cloud over gRPC and a Bearer-authenticated candidate over HTTP:


```text
receivers  :
otlp  :
protocols  :
grpc  :
endpoint  :   0.0.0.0  :  4317
http  :
endpoint  :   0.0.0.0  :  4318


processors  :
batch  :


exporters  :
otlp_grpc/laminar  :
endpoint  :   api.lmnr.ai  :  8443
headers  :
authorization  :     "Bearer ${env:LMNR_PROJECT_API_KEY}"
otlp_http/candidate  :
endpoint  :   $  {  env  :  CANDIDATE_OTLP_ENDPOINT  }
headers  :
authorization  :     "Bearer ${env:CANDIDATE_API_KEY}"


service  :
pipelines  :
traces  :
receivers  :     [  otlp  ]
processors  :     [  batch  ]
exporters  :     [  otlp_grpc/laminar  ,   otlp_http/candidate  ]


```


Point the application's exporter at the Collector. Replace the candidate endpoint and headers with its documented settings; this authentication block is not universal. Langfuse uses Basic authentication, and its docs add an ingestion-version header so OTLP data isn't processed with a delay. Laminar's gRPC metadata requires lowercase authorization


, as documented in the[OTLP reference](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/otel) .


Collector 0.166.0 accepts otlp_grpc


and otlp_http


. Its older aliases, otlp


and otlphttp


, still validate but produce deprecation warnings.


The local test used Collector 0.166.0, Laminar OSS and Phoenix 22.0.1. The application used plain OpenTelemetry with GenAI attributes supplied manually. Phoenix initially rejected export with HTTP 401; its exporter dropped 12 spans while Laminar received all 12. After authentication was disabled for the local Phoenix test, both received two traces containing 12 spans, with matching token totals and the tool error. This tested transport and supplied-field mapping, not automatic framework instrumentation.


### Option 2: use an SDK bridge#


For an existing Langfuse application, Laminar's[Langfuse bridge](https://laminar.sh/docs/integrations/langfuse) adds a receiving copy:


```text
from   lmnr   import   Laminar


Laminar  .  initialize  (  bridges  =  [  "langfuse"  ]  )


from   langfuse   import   observe
from   langfuse  .  openai   import   OpenAI


```


Set LMNR_PROJECT_API_KEY


. Existing @observe


functions and the Langfuse OpenAI wrapper remain in place. The bridge documentation states that Langfuse keeps its original spans and attributes while Laminar processes its own copy.


Supported versions are Python langfuse


3.x–5.x with lmnr


0.9.0+, and TypeScript @langfuse/*


4.x–6.x with @lmnr-ai/lmnr


0.9.1+. The bridge does not forward Vercel AI SDK calls; those need Laminar's AI SDK integration separately.


The test used langfuse


5.2.0 and lmnr


0.9.2. The Langfuse destination was a local capture endpoint, not a running Langfuse server or UI. That endpoint and Laminar received matching trace IDs and six spans per run. Token totals matched: 457 input/57 output and 440 input/76 output. Laminar also mapped user, session, tags and customer metadata, and preserved the create_po


error message.


### Option 3: add a span processor#


If you own the tracer provider, retain your exporter and add Laminar's processor. A minimal TypeScript setup is:


```text
import     {   NodeSDK   }     from     "@opentelemetry/sdk-node"  ;
import     {   BatchSpanProcessor   }     from     "@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base"  ;
import     {   OTLPTraceExporter   }     from     "@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-proto"  ;
import     {   LaminarSpanProcessor   }     from     "@lmnr-ai/lmnr"  ;


const   sdk   =     new     NodeSDK  (  {
spanProcessors  :     [
new     BatchSpanProcessor  (  new     OTLPTraceExporter  (  )  )  ,
new     LaminarSpanProcessor  (  )  ,
]  ,
}  )  ;
sdk  .  start  (  )  ;


```


Keep your current exporter's configuration in the first processor. The second reads LMNR_PROJECT_API_KEY


and defaults to Laminar Cloud. The Python SDK also exports LaminarSpanProcessor


, added through provider.add_span_processor()


.


Local Python and TypeScript tests sent the spans to both Phoenix and Laminar using this pattern. Use your own runtime and package versions for the trial's capture checks.


## Select runs and apply one protocol#


Choose trace IDs before comparing interfaces. Start with 10–20 runs that cover your longest contexts, known errors, expensive executions and incorrect outcomes reported as success. Expand the sample if it misses a workload you need to support.


Check attribute mapping before scoring. In the Collector test, a plain root-span customer_id


remained a span attribute in Laminar; trace metadata was empty. Setting lmnr.association.properties.metadata.customer_id


populated trace[metadata](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/structure/metadata) . Langfuse's equivalent trace-metadata key is langfuse.trace.metadata.customer_id


.


Apply necessary mappings to every candidate, including your current tool. A field stored in the wrong place is not evidence of a missing product capability.


Check Procedure Record


Capture completeness Inspect longest runs Missing spans, truncated content


Failure investigation Diagnose known-bad runs Time, failing step, cause


Cost accuracy Reconcile comparable usage Unexplained cost difference


Team questions Answer the agreed questions Answer, effort, workaround


Evaluation workflow Convert three bad runs Steps, retained data


Expected bill Price measured volume Current and 3× estimates


Residency and retention Check deployment and plan Location, accessible history


Compare captured spans with application-side expectations, not just with the other backend: both could omit the same data. Inspect tool arguments and results as well as span counts.


For investigation timing, use equally familiar reviewers or give each reviewer equivalent onboarding. Rotate tool order to reduce learning effects. Time the task rather than assuming that one interface is faster; the local tests here did not measure debugging time.


For cost reconciliation, isolate the same models, account and time window on both sides. Separate untraced calls, discounts and special token rates before judging the remaining difference. Agree on an acceptable tolerance for your use case rather than applying a universal percentage.


Record hard requirements as pass/fail and keep timings, counts and workarounds visible. Set priorities before seeing results so a convenient demo does not outweigh a missing production requirement.


## Work through the questions in Laminar#


The procurement-agent tests demonstrate ingestion, metadata mapping and SQL queries. They do not establish a usability winner or production-scale completeness.


### Find the failing operation#


Open the copied trace and locate create_po


. The[transcript view](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/viewing-traces) reads top to bottom: the user's request ("Order 2 27in monitors"), each model turn, and the search_catalog


and create_po


calls inline with their arguments and results. The last turn is the agent offering to search other suppliers. The span tree is one click away when you need the call hierarchy and timing. The local bridge test stored both the span's error status and the message supplier Contoso: account on credit hold


. During your trial, check whether the transcript provides enough preceding context to explain that failure without returning to application logs.


### Query customer costs and repeated tools#


The customer-cost query ran against the local stack through the SQL API. You can use the same query in the[SQL editor](https://laminar.sh/docs/platform/sql-editor) :


```text
SELECT
JSONExtractString  (  metadata  ,     'customer_id'  )     AS   customer  ,
count  (  )     AS   runs  ,
countIf  (  status     =     'error'  )     AS   failed  ,
round  (  sum  (  total_cost  )  ,     4  )     AS   cost_usd
FROM   traces
WHERE   start_time   >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     7     DAY
GROUP     BY   customer
ORDER     BY   cost_usd   DESC


```


To find runs that repeatedly search the catalog:


```text
SELECT   trace_id  ,   countIf  (  name   =     'search_catalog'  )     AS   searches
FROM   spans
WHERE   span_type   =     'TOOL'     AND   start_time   >     now  (  )     -     INTERVAL     7     DAY
GROUP     BY   trace_id
HAVING   searches   >     5
ORDER     BY   searches   DESC


```


The small local sample exercised this query with HAVING searches >= 1


. The threshold above is the proposed trial criterion, not an observed loop in that sample.


For one gpt-4.1-mini


run, Laminar reported $0.000274 for 457 input and 57 output tokens. That matches arithmetic using $0.40 per million input tokens and $1.60 per million output tokens. It is a list-price check, not reconciliation against a provider invoice.


### Test detection of incorrect outcomes#


An illustrative wrong-quantity run needs evaluation beyond error status. With Signals, you can analyze traces using an instruction and JSON schema, producing structured events. A trial instruction could ask: “Did the purchase-order quantity differ from the user's requested quantity?”


Test that instruction against labeled correct and incorrect orders, and review missed failures as well as false alarms. This Signal was not exercised in the OSS tests. It requires Laminar Cloud Pro or Scale, or enterprise-licensed self-hosting, and usage belongs in the trial budget.


### Keep product gaps in the decision#


Laminar has no prompt management comparable to Langfuse or LangSmith, and no host metrics or APM. If those workflows are mandatory, retain another tool or choose accordingly. For a single model call without tools, Laminar's agent-specific workflows may add little.


## Estimate the bill from trial volume#


Measure daily spans, traces and billable data volume, then price each candidate in its own unit. Raw payload bytes are not interchangeable with compressed billable bytes. The[observability pricing guide](https://laminar.sh/article/llm-observability-pricing) explains the different billing models.


Estimate today's workload and a 3× workload as a sensitivity check, not a growth prediction. Include evaluation or analysis charges alongside ingestion, and check whether longer runs change the mix of spans and bytes.


As of November 25, 2026,[Laminar's pricing](https://laminar.sh/pricing) bills data after compression:


Plan Monthly base Included data Overage Data access


Free $0 1 GB None 7 days


Pro $30 3 GB $2/GB 3 months


Scale $250 100 GB $1/GB 1 year


Pro charges Signals usage per token; Scale includes $50 of Signals credit per billing cycle. Free does not include Signals.


Check how far back investigations must reach before choosing retention. For residency requirements, evaluate the complete deployment and any external processing. Laminar supports[Docker Compose and Helm self-hosting](https://laminar.sh/docs/self-hosting/overview) , with tracing, search, dashboards and evaluations available across deployment options.


## FAQ#


### Does exporting to two backends add application latency?#


It can add overhead, so benchmark your configuration rather than assuming the effect is negligible. Batch span processors export in the background, but serialization, buffering and network work still consume resources. Compare application latency, CPU and memory under the same workload before and during dual export.


### What happens when a candidate stays unavailable?#


You can lose its copy when retries expire or its sending queue fills. Collector exporter defaults include a queue size of 1,000 and a maximum retry time of 300 seconds. Separate exporters do not guarantee unlimited failure isolation; monitor export errors and dropped data throughout the trial.


### Why can matching token totals produce different costs?#


Backends can apply different model rates or interpret special token categories differently. Laminar uses gen_ai.response.model


when available and falls back to gen_ai.request.model


. Check model aliases, cached-token pricing and custom rates in the[cost-tracking documentation](https://laminar.sh/docs/tracing/cost-tracking) .


### How do I match trace IDs displayed in different formats?#


Compare their underlying hexadecimal value rather than punctuation. In the bridge test, Laminar SQL displayed cb6c111b-4704-3397-9aef-7b025a771173


, while the capture endpoint used the same ID without hyphens. Normalize that representation when building your trial's run list.


### What should a regression case retain from a trial trace?#


Keep the expected outcome and grading rule alongside the inputs and relevant execution context. A failing trace records what happened, not what should happen. Remove unnecessary sensitive data and confirm that the edited case still reproduces the failure; the[trace-to-evaluation-dataset guide](https://laminar.sh/article/production-traces-to-eval-dataset) covers the Laminar workflow.
